title: Cover

segs.cue: you've already introduced yourself; start straight on the cover

segs.t: So my project is called Poise. It helps you notice when your posture drifts, without breaking your focus. I made a web app and a light bar that sits on your monitor.

I picked this project for two reasons. First, it shows the whole process, from research to design, testing and iteration, so you can see what I changed at each step. Second, I used AI all the way through, so I can show you how it helped me make decisions.
So, let me walk you through it.

title: We drift without noticing

segs.cue: quick: one short line per press

segs.t: This is how I define the problem in one sentence. We drift without noticing.
At first, we sit up straight.
Then sometimes, we rest our chin on our hand.
Bit by bit, we lean in closer to the screen.
Over time, the neck and lower back start to hurt.
And fixing it later can cost thousands. I've had neck and back pain myself, and spent a lot on physical therapy and a good chair. And I wasn't the only one.

kw: “We drift without noticing.”
Sit up straight
Chin on hand
Lean closer
Neck + lower back hurt
Costs thousands
Me: PT + a good chair

title: Six hours a day

segs.t: So I looked at some research to see if other people feel the same. The average US adult sits about six hours a day. Up to 63 percent of office workers get neck pain in a year. And back and neck pain is the biggest health cost in the US, about 135 billion dollars.
So yeah, it's not just me.

kw: Research → others too?
6 hours sitting a day
Up to 63% neck pain in a year
$135 billion, biggest health cost
“So yeah, it's not just me.”

title: Survey

segs.t: Then I ran a quick survey with fifteen people.

Three things stood out. Nine out of fifteen rarely notice their posture, or only once it hurts. Fourteen feel pain after a long session, mostly in the neck and lower back. And most of what they'd tried, like stretching or a better chair, comes after. So nothing really catches it early.

kw: Survey, 15 people → three things
9/15 rarely notice, or once it hurts
14 feel pain → neck, lower back
Fixes come after → nothing catches it early

title: Interviews

segs.t: To go deeper, I interviewed three of them, Paul, Hyunjoo and Peter.
So, Paul only notices he's slouching when his lower back starts to hurt.
Hyunjoo bought a Herman Miller chair. It helped at first, but sitting straight for long was still hard.
And Peter leans toward the screen when he focuses. He works in quiet places, so a silent reminder would help him.
So I found an opportunity for each of them.
For Paul, I can help him notice earlier.
For Hyunjoo, I can give him short breaks to reset and sit well again.
And for Peter, I can give him a signal that doesn't interrupt him.

kw: Interviewed Paul, Hyunjoo, Peter
Paul → notices when lower back hurts
Hyunjoo → Herman Miller, still hard to sit straight
Peter → leans in when focused, quiet places
One opportunity each
Paul → notice earlier
Hyunjoo → short breaks to reset
Peter → signal that doesn't interrupt

title: Market research

segs.t: Next I looked at what's already out there. Posture apps notice early, but they interrupt your work, and chairs and Pilates come after it already hurts. So I wanted to catch it early, without interrupting.

I also like seeing what I can bring in from other services. On DoorDash, I can see my order on the lock screen without opening the app, and Uber, Starbucks and Nike Run Club work the same way. So I could show people their posture live.

→ catch it early, without interrupting

title: Hypothesis

segs.t: So from all three, I needed to help people notice early, with a clear cue that doesn't interrupt them.
So I thought, if people get a clear cue that helps them notice early, with no interruptions, they'll catch the drift sooner and stay aligned longer.

So for the user, I wanted the app to tell you when you drift and the light bar to change color as you move, so you notice it without stopping your work. And for the business, I'd keep the app free so people can try it first, then offer the light bar. Seeing their posture get better over time would turn it into a daily habit.

kw: Notice early + clear cue + no interruption
Hypothesis → catch drift sooner, stay aligned longer
User → app tells you, light changes color
Business → free app first, then light bar → daily habit

title: User flow

segs.t: Here's how it works in five steps.
First, you answer four questions, pick the camera or the sensor, and plug in the light bar.
Then you start working. The app checks your posture and the light stays white.
If you drift, the app shows what changed and the light turns yellow, then red. When you sit back up, it turns green and fades back to white.
When you finish, a report shows how long you sat well.
Then you take a break with stretches or a game, and the light plays along.

kw: Five steps
① 4 questions, camera or sensor, plug in
② Work → light stays white
③ Drift → yellow, red → sit up → green → white
④ Report → how long you sat well
⑤ Break → stretches or game, light plays along

title: Version one, the app

segs.cue: the recording plays; press once per part

segs.t: So here's how it works, in four parts.

First, onboarding. Poise asks four questions, like how long you focus, how it should tell you when you drift, what helps you rest, and if breaks should start on their own. I came up with this from the interviews, because everyone worked differently, so setup starts from your own answers.

Next is focus mode. The bar on the right fills up as you drift, and the label tells you how you moved. And the light bar turns yellow, then red, and green when you sit back up. And at the end, a report shows how long you stayed aligned.
I came up with this from the survey, because nine out of fifteen only noticed once it hurt, so the bar reacts right away.
Then break mode. This figure shows you each stretch, and the camera checks how closely you match it as a percent. Up top, you can switch to a reset or a small game.
I came up with this from the survey too, because a lot of people stretch to fix their posture, so I made this break mode to help them reset.
And last, settings. In this modal, you can change your modes, how bright the light bar glows, and the music.
I came up with this from the interviews, because everyone has different preferences, so there are a few options to choose from.

Focus mode → bar fills as you drift, label shows how
Light → yellow, red, green

title: Playtest

segs.t: This is also part of my school project, so I showed my app and the light bar to my classmates, and I mostly watched and took notes.

kw: School project → showed classmates
Mostly watched + took notes

title: What the playtest showed

segs.t: And watching people use it changed what I thought mattered.
On the good side, it caught people slouching before they even noticed, and they loved having options for a break. So it caught drift early, and gave people control.

But from the light alone, they couldn't tell how they moved. Twelve guide steps felt like too much, and some worried what the camera collects. So setup was slow and the light wasn't clear. And people wanted to feel safe with the camera.
And for new ideas, they wanted to just type the mode they want, and keep a small window open while they work. So they wanted it their own way, and always in view.

kw: “Watching people changed what I thought mattered.”
Good → caught slouching before they noticed, break options → early + control
Bad → light alone unclear, 12 steps, camera worry
→ slow setup, unclear light, feel safe
New ideas → type the mode, small window
→ their way, always in view

title: Iteration plan

segs.t: So I planned the next version from two places.

From my classmates, the biggest one was privacy. The app already said the camera never records, but it was too small, so people missed it. So I'll make the modal clearly show how your privacy is protected, and that there's a sensor option too. The trade off is, the sensor is less accurate than the camera.
Next, clearer cues. I thought the light bar was enough, but it wasn't, so I'll add a voice that tells you how to fix it when you drift. The trade off is, a voice can interrupt you.
And people wanted it simpler and more their own. So I'll add a text bar called Ask Poise to change settings, a mini window and a shorter guide. The trade off is, more features, more to learn.
From my own review, I'll add a figure that moves with you, and keep the number. The trade off is, the figure is less exact, and the number is smaller.
I'll use one design system, since version one looked uneven. The trade off is, edge cases need new rules and can limit creativity.
And I'll take the green out, since going back to white already shows you're sitting well. The trade off is, the feedback when you sit back up is less clear.

kw: Plan from two places
Classmates:
Privacy → note was too small → modal → clearly show how privacy is protected + sensor option ↔ sensor less accurate
Clearer cues → light wasn't enough → voice ↔ can interrupt
Simpler, their own → Ask Poise, mini window, short guide ↔ more to learn
My review:
Figure that moves + keep number ↔ less exact, smaller
One design system ↔ edge cases, less creativity
No green → white = good ↔ feedback for sitting up less clear

title: Same five steps

segs.t: So I built version two with the same five steps, and you can see what I changed in green. Set up has a clearer camera or sensor choice. Focus adds a figure and a mini window. And when you drift, a voice tells you how to fix it, and the light goes yellow, red, and back to white. In the report, you can hover the chart for each moment. And in the break, the same figure now shows up in every game.

title: Version two, the app

segs.cue: the recording plays; press once per change

segs.t: So here's version two. There are six changes, so I'll go quickly.

First, camera or sensor. So now, before you start, Poise tells you how each one works. The camera never records you, and the sensor just checks how far you sit from the screen. I came up with this from the playtest, because people were worried about the camera, and didn't really know what the sensor was for.

Next, simpler steps. I grouped the twelve guide steps by topic into four, so each one is easier to understand. And changing a mode is now a short side panel, not a long list of sliders. I came up with this from the playtest, because twelve steps was too much before even starting.

Then, easier to notice. A figure moves with you, the card changes color as you drift, and a voice tells you how to fix it. And in the report, you can hover the chart to see what moved. I came up with this from the playtest, because people couldn't tell what the bar and the number meant, and the light alone wasn't enough to notice.

This is the mini window. You can use Poise in a small window over your other tabs, so you keep tracking while you work. I came up with this from the playtest, because people wanted to keep tracking their posture while they work, even in a small view on other tabs.

And this is Ask Poise. I added a text field where you can just type what you want, like a one hour focus with breathing breaks, and Poise sets it up for you. I came up with this from the playtest, because people had a hard time finding settings, and wanted it their own way.

And last, one look and feel. To make it feel more polished, I carefully adjusted the typography, color and spacing, and set rules for each, so it all became one design system. I came up with this from my own review, because I built it with AI, so the color, typography and spacing didn't match. Now it feels like one product.

title: Testing version two

segs.t: Then I tested version two with Paul, Hyunjoo and Peter at their own desks, for an hour each.
Overall, people liked the small changes, like the figure that follows you and the little window. So it helped without breaking focus.
But when Peter was on a call, the voice told him to sit up in the middle of it, and he had to leave the little window just to take a break. So it got in the way of calls and breaks.
And there were some new ideas, like having the voice go quiet during meetings, or seeing when they slouch the most each week. So people want it to fit their day and habits.

kw: v2 → Paul, Hyunjoo, Peter, own desks, 1 hour
Good → figure, little window → no broken focus
Bad → Peter's call, voice cut in; left window for break
New → quiet in meetings, weekly slouch times
→ fit their day and habits

title: Then I measured it

segs.t: Then I measured it, with the same three people, and they did the same things in version one and version two.

The one I cared about most was time aligned, because my hypothesis was that people would catch the drift sooner and stay aligned longer. It went from 85 to 90 percent. That might sound small, but everyone already sat well most of the time. All three went up, and Peter, who drifted the most, improved the most.
So they stayed aligned longer, and it got easier to use.

kw: Same 3 people, same tasks, v1 vs v2
Cared most about time aligned
Hypothesis → catch drift sooner, stay aligned longer
Small, but already sat well
All 3 up, Peter most
→ aligned longer, easier to use

title: What I learned using AI

segs.t: Now, what I learned using AI, since I used it at almost every step.

In research, I only had one month, and I wanted to spend most of it talking to people and hearing their stories. So AI found papers and drafted my questions. But I read each paper myself and organized the questions. So AI finds and drafts fast, but judging what fits is still my job.

When building, I wanted a real app to test within days, so AI coded the app and the Arduino from my flow. Then I had people try each build and watched them drift. So AI lets me build real things, but only users know if it helps them.

And for testing, I wanted to spend my time watching people use a real app, not a mockup, so AI read the posture data from every session, like how long they stayed aligned and how often they drifted, and compared version one and two. But I still checked every number myself against each session. And that way, I could catch things the data can't show, like when the voice cut into Peter's call. So AI can read the data, but only I can see how people really use it.

So yeah, overall, AI can boost your ideas, but it still needs a human to check and judge its work, because AI can make mistakes, and it can't see the full context or your big picture. So I think the best way to use AI is to treat it as your design assistant that you can discuss ideas with, and not let it do your work for you.
